label: Breaks and time off
rationale: Stepping away from work, commonest first: missing a day, booking leave, a short break, quitting for good.
mixUps: yasumu (stay off) and yameru (quit) sound alike; yasumi o toru is days off, while a few minutes' rest is kyuukei o toru.

targets.english: take time off work, miss work
targets.verbSense: rest, take a break; stay away from (work, school)
targets.trap: yasumu sounds like 'rest', and 'off work' or 'from work' suggests kara, giving shigoto kara yasumu. Work is the object: shigoto o yasumu, like gakkou o yasumu (miss school). yasumi o toru (take time off) is also fine.
targets.use: Said when you stay away from work, sick or not, for a day or longer: kyou shigoto yasumu. It's usually heard in the past (yasunda), and gakkou o yasumu works the same way.
targets.notes: Planned leave is yasumi o toru. 'I'm off tomorrow' is just ashita yasumi.

example.ja: 今日風邪で仕事休んだ。
example.english: I took today off work with a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaze de shigoto o yasumimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は風邪で仕事を休みました。
examplePolite.english: I took today off work with a cold.

targets.verbSense: take; get (here: take time away from work, booked ahead or on the spot)
targets.trap: 'Take a break' for a few minutes isn't yasumi o toru, which on its own means time off, or rest in general (chanto yasumi totte ne, make sure you get some rest). For a few minutes, say chotto yasumou, kyuukei shiyou or kyuukei torou.
targets.use: Said about days off arranged with work, usually once they're booked: raishuu yasumi totta. The o is often dropped, and paid leave works the same way: yuukyuu totta. The everyday complaint is yasumi torenai (I can't get time off).
targets.notes: A sick day is yasumu instead: kyou kaze de yasumu.

example.romaji: raishuu mikka yasumi totta n da.
example.ja: 来週三日休み取ったんだ。
example.english: I've booked three days off next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu mikka yasumi o totta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週三日休みを取ったんです。
examplePolite.english: I've booked three days off next week.

targets.trap: 'Take a break' tempts yasumi o toru, which means time off or proper rest (chanto yasumi totte ne). A few minutes' break is kyuukei: kyuukei torou.
targets.use: Said about breaks at work or while studying, especially the ones you're owed: chanto kyuukei totte ne, juppun kyuukei torou. Casual speech drops o, and for calling a break on the spot kyuukei shiyou or chotto yasumou is more common.
targets.notes: On a break right now: ima kyuukei-chuu. Going on your break at work is kyuukei ni hairu: kyuukei hairimasu.

example.ja: ちゃんと休憩取ってね。
example.english: Make sure you take your breaks.

examplePolite.romaji: chanto kyuukei o totte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちゃんと休憩を取ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Make sure you take your breaks.

targets.verbSense: quit, leave (a job, school or club); same sound as yameru 'stop'
targets.trap: 'Leave the company' suggests kaisha o deru, but that normally means walking out of the office building (going home, heading out to lunch). Leaving the job is kaisha o yameru. Likewise daigaku o deru means graduating; dropping out is yameru.
targets.use: Said about leaving a job for good, mostly as yameta (I quit) or as a complaint, yametai (I want to quit). Casual speech drops o, and shigoto o yameru means the same.
targets.notes: Getting fired is kubi ni naru: kubi ni natta.

example.english: I quit my job last year.

examplePolite.romaji: kyonen kaisha o yameta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 去年会社を辞めたんです。
examplePolite.english: I quit my job last year.
